what: Spatial and Mean-Field Forest-Fire Invasion Model
title: Spatial and Mean-Field Forest-Fire Invasion Model
text: R package simulating two-species vegetation system fire mediates competition native species invader. continuous-time transition rules simulated three ways: explicit lattice Gillespie algorithm, deterministic well-mixed (mean-field) limit, well-mixed stochastic process finite population size. engine written C++ exposed R Rcpp, interface built around dimensionless parameters (xi, eta, p) fire spread, post-fire regrowth clustering initial landscape. model documented inside package: help("ForestFireR-model") defines five states, every transition rate, dimensionless parametrization, baseline parameter set fire-mediated invasion mechanism encodes, mean-field equations, differs three engines.

title: Spatial and Mean-Field Forest-Fire Invasion Model
text: Starting 10 per cent invader baseline parameters (xi_nat = 0.5, xi_inv = eta_inv = 0.6, eta_nat = 0) 200 years: Mean field (n1_0 = 0.9, n2_0 = 0.1): native declines 0.90 0.079 invader grows 0.10 0.613. Lattice (L = 100, density2 = 0.1, p = 1, seed = 1): native ends 0.050 invader 0.675; run scattered invader (p = 0) ends 0.057 native 0.336 invader, rest grid still unoccupied post-fire ground. Well mixed, stochastic (N = 10000): invasion take (native 0.971, invader 0.029 T = 200). Fire discrete, rare event, whereas deterministic limit carries residual burning density order 1e-11 times, keeps feedback running; without fire native species -replaces invader construction. Sweeping xi_inv eta_inv (inst/examples/03_phase_diagram_xi_eta_sweep.R) maps transition native extinction plane two fire-mediated advantages. Mass conservation (n1+n2+n3+n4+n5 = 1) holds floating-point precision three engines: largest deviation recorded L = 100, T = 200 trajectory 1.1e-16. testthat suite checks exact, priori known outcomes (null dynamics, single-species colonization, isolated fire burnout, ignition switched , reproducibility, mass conservation, xi/eta conversion, random stream ).

title: Named grid-state codes — FF_STATE
text: integer codes used LxL grids returned/accepted generate_landscape(), generate_landscape_layers() simulate_spatial_from_grid(): 1 = native vegetation (\(V^{nat}\)), 2 = invader vegetation (\(V^{inv}\)), 3 = active fire (\(F\)), 4 = unoccupied, never-yet-burned space (\(\emptyset\)), 5 = unoccupied, post-fire space (\(\emptyset^F\), one two unoccupied states long-range regrowth channel, via eta_nat/eta_inv; baseline parametrization sets eta_nat = 0, leaving invader regrowth advantage ). what: Baseline parameters and the invasion mechanism
title: The fire-driven invasion model simulated by ForestFireR — ForestFireR-model
text: default_rates() returns baseline set, time years: \(\lambda_{\emptyset nat} = \lambda_{\emptyset inv} = 0.03\), \(\lambda_{nat\,inv} = 0.005\), \(\lambda_{inv\,nat} = 0.01\), \(\lambda^{F\emptyset} = 10^6\), \(\lambda^{ig}_{nat} = 0\), \(\lambda^{ig}_{inv} = 10^{-4}\), \(\xi_{nat} = 0.5\), \(\xi_{inv} = 0.6\), \(\eta_{nat} = 0\), \(\eta_{inv} = 0.6\). values make competition asymmetric native species' favour: native replaces invader twice fast reverse (\(\lambda_{inv\,nat} = 2 \lambda_{nat\,inv}\)), two colonise unoccupied space equally well, without fire invader spread. advantages act fire: species ignites spontaneously, carries fire better (\(\xi_{inv} > \xi_{nat}\)), one regrows post-fire sites long-range channel (\(\eta_{inv} > \eta_{nat} = 0\)). Fire converts native vegetation \(\emptyset^F\), invader claims preferentially, raises amount fire-prone vegetation: invasion fire reinforce . \(\xi_{inv}\) \(\eta_{inv}\) strength feedback, parameters analyses vary. Fire also much faster vegetation: \(\lambda^{F\emptyset} = 10^6\)/year site burns half hour, decades vegetation turns . single outbreak therefore resolves sliver simulated time (see capture_fire_snapshots simulate_spatial() observe one).

title: The fire-driven invasion model simulated by ForestFireR — ForestFireR-model
text: simulate_mean_field() integrates well-mixed limit transitions, neighbour count \(v_X\) replaced global density \(n_X\): $$\dot n_1 = \lambda_{\emptyset nat} n_1 (n_4 + n_5) + \lambda^{rg}_{nat} n_5 + \lambda_{inv\,nat} n_1 n_2 - \lambda_{nat\,inv} n_1 n_2 - (\lambda^{ig}_{nat} + \lambda^{sp}_{nat} n_3) n_1$$ $$\dot n_2 = \lambda_{\emptyset inv} n_2 (n_4 + n_5) + \lambda^{rg}_{inv} n_5 + \lambda_{nat\,inv} n_1 n_2 - \lambda_{inv\,nat} n_1 n_2 - (\lambda^{ig}_{inv} + \lambda^{sp}_{inv} n_3) n_2$$ $$\dot n_3 = (\lambda^{ig}_{nat} + \lambda^{sp}_{nat} n_3) n_1 + (\lambda^{ig}_{inv} + \lambda^{sp}_{inv} n_3) n_2 - \lambda^{F\emptyset} n_3$$ $$\dot n_4 = -(\lambda_{\emptyset nat} n_1 + \lambda_{\emptyset inv} n_2) n_4$$ $$\dot n_5 = \lambda^{F\emptyset} n_3 - (\lambda_{\emptyset nat} n_1 + \lambda_{\emptyset inv} n_2) n_5 - (\lambda^{rg}_{nat} + \lambda^{rg}_{inv}) n_5$$ (vegetation death terms, zero R interface, omitted). Fire enters continuous density: \(n_3\) settles \((\lambda^{ig}_{nat} n_1 + \lambda^{ig}_{inv} n_2)/(\lambda^{F\emptyset} - \lambda^{sp}_{nat} n_1 - \lambda^{sp}_{inv} n_2)\), order \(10^{-11}\) baseline parameters – tiny, always burning, feedback runs continuously. lattice finite-N versions fire instead discrete, rare event. difference, rather presence absence space alone, three engines can disagree.

text: Integrates mean-field ODE system describing well-mixed limit model returns full trajectory data frame. equations written ForestFireR-model. fire compartment advanced exact linear solution step vegetation block integrated classic RK4, keeps integration stable default L_30 = 1e6 (explicit fixed-step RK4 fire term alone diverges practical step size).

code: # Invasion trajectory on a 80x80 grid over 150 years r <- simulate_spatial(T = 150, L = 80, density2 = 0.05, p = 1,                       xi_inv = 0.6, eta_inv = 0.6,                       record_dt = 1, seed = 1) plot(r$trajectory$time, r$trajectory$n1, type = "l", col = "forestgreen",      ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "time (years)", ylab = "density") lines(r$trajectory$time, r$trajectory$n2, col = "firebrick") legend("right", c("native", "invader"), lty = 1, bty = "n",        col = c("forestgreen", "firebrick"))   # Final densities only -- the fast option for parameter sweeps simulate_spatial(T = 150, L = 80, seed = 1)[c("n1", "n2", "n5")] #> $n1 #> [1] 0.0590625 #>  #> $n2 #> [1] 0.7575 #>  #> $n5 #> [1] 0.1832813 #>   # Initial and final grids g <- simulate_spatial(T = 150, L = 80, record_grid = TRUE, seed = 1) image(g$final_grid, col = c("forestgreen", "firebrick", "orange",                             "grey90", "grey60"), axes = FALSE)

title: Simulate the spatially-explicit model from a supplied landscape — simulate_spatial_from_grid
text: Like simulate_spatial(), starts initial grid supply (typically generate_landscape_layers()) instead building one internally density2/p. Use initial condition generate_landscape() express , typically alongside rate constants zeroed isolate subset dynamics. Two useful recipes: study post-fire regrowth/colonization isolation, disable fire entirely (xi_nat = 0, xi_inv = 0, Lig_23 = 0) vegetation replacement (L_12 = 0, L_21 = 0); study fire spread isolation (e.g. starting small ignition patch -invader domain), disable colonization/regrowth (L_01 = 0, L_02 = 0, eta_inv = 0) native-side reactions (irrelevant native vegetation initial condition), keeping fire spread/burnout.

title: Simulate the spatially-explicit model from a supplied landscape — simulate_spatial_from_grid
code: # Post-fire regrowth in isolation: both species scattered over an empty # post-fire domain, with fire and competitive replacement switched off. g <- generate_landscape_layers(L = 60, fill_state = FF_STATE["empty_postfire"],   layers = list(     list(background = FF_STATE["empty_postfire"], pattern = FF_STATE["native"],          density = 0.05, p = 0.8),     list(background = FF_STATE["empty_postfire"], pattern = FF_STATE["invader"],          density = 0.05, p = 0.8)   ), seed = 1) r <- simulate_spatial_from_grid(T = 300, initial_grid = g,                                 xi_nat = 0, xi_inv = 0, Lig_23 = 0,                                 L_12 = 0, L_21 = 0,                                 record_dt = 10, seed = 1) tail(r$trajectory, 1)        # the invader's eta_inv claims the burnt ground #>       time n0         n1        n2 n3 n4 n5 #> 8 64.71132  0 0.08666667 0.9133333  0  0  0  # Fire spread in isolation: an ignition patch over an all-invader domain, # with no native vegetation, so the extinction stop has to be turned off. g2 <- generate_landscape_layers(L = 60, fill_state = FF_STATE["invader"],   layers = list(     list(background = FF_STATE["invader"], pattern = FF_STATE["fire"],          density = 0.01, p = 0.8)   ), seed = 1) f <- simulate_spatial_from_grid(T = 1e-4, initial_grid = g2,                                 xi_inv = 0.8, eta_inv = 0,                                 L_01 = 0, L_02 = 0, L_12 = 0, L_21 = 0,                                 Lig_23 = 0, check_extinction = FALSE,                                 record_grid = TRUE, seed = 1) c(fire = f$n3, burnt = f$n5) #>      fire     burnt  #> 0.0000000 0.9991667

code: if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{ # Needs the 'av' package: install.packages("av") # T chosen large enough for these default rates to actually do # something visible -- see Details. path <- simulate_spatial_movie(T = 150, L = 80, density2 = 0.05, p = 1,                                 n_frames = 150, fps = 15,                                 file = "invasion.mp4", seed = 1)  # Needs the 'gifski' package: install.packages("gifski") simulate_spatial_movie(T = 150, L = 60, n_frames = 80,                         file = "invasion.gif", seed = 1)  # Fire spread, seeded directly. The default L_30 = 1e6 resolves a fire in # ~1e-4 years, invisible to any video, so both the burnout rate and T are # rescaled here to the duration of a real fire in one cell (see the # fire-spread-only recipe in simulate_spatial_from_grid()'s examples). # L_30 = 5500/year corresponds to ~1.6 h per 30x30 m cell, which two # independent estimates support: understory fire rate-of-spread in # tropical forest, ~1-3 m/min, takes ~10-30 min to cross 30 m; and # Saravia et al. 2025 (Oikos, doi:10.1111/oik.10764) fit a contact-spread # fire model -- the same mechanism as this package's fire rule -- on a # 460 m/pixel Amazon grid with a fixed one-day fire duration per site, # which rescales linearly by the cell-size ratio (460/30 ~ 15) to ~1.6 h. # T is rescaled to ~15 days to match, so the fire front stays visible # across frames. xi_inv still sets the spread-vs-burnout probability # exactly as documented in xi2lambda(). ignite <- generate_landscape_layers(   L = 80, fill_state = FF_STATE["invader"],   layers = list(list(background = FF_STATE["invader"],                       pattern = FF_STATE["fire"], density = 0.01, p = 1)),   seed = 1 ) simulate_spatial_movie(T = 0.04, initial_grid = ignite,                         xi_nat = 0, xi_inv = 0.8, eta_inv = 0,                         L_01 = 0, L_02 = 0, L_12 = 0, L_21 = 0,                         Lig_13 = 0, Lig_23 = 0, L_30 = 5500,                         check_extinction = FALSE,                         n_frames = 150, fps = 20,                         file = "fire_spread.mp4", seed = 1) } # }

what: Convert a spread or regrowth probability to a rate constant — xi2lambda
title: Convert a spread or regrowth probability to a rate constant — xi2lambda
text: model parametrizes fire spread post-fire regrowth two dimensionless probabilities: \(\xi\), probability burning neighbour ignites given vegetation type fire burns , \(\eta\), probability unoccupied post-fire site regrows given species recolonised way. convert rate constant relation, obtained setting \(\xi = \lambda^{sp}/(\lambda^{sp}+\lambda^{F\emptyset})\) (analogously \(\eta\)) solving rate: $$\lambda = \frac{\xi}{1-\xi}\,\lambda_{ref}$$

title: Convert a spread or regrowth probability to a rate constant — xi2lambda
code: xi2lambda(xi, lambda_ref)  eta2lambda(xi, lambda_ref)

title: Convert a spread or regrowth probability to a rate constant — xi2lambda
text: xi Probability [0, 1) (named xi fire spread, eta regrowth – use formula). lambda_ref reference rate probability defined (L_30, .e. \(\lambda^{F\emptyset}\), fire spread; L_01, .e. \(\lambda_{\emptyset nat}\), regrowth – see Details).

title: Convert a spread or regrowth probability to a rate constant — xi2lambda
text: corresponding rate constant (units lambda_ref).

title: Convert a spread or regrowth probability to a rate constant — xi2lambda
text: Fire spread: xi2lambda(xi_nat, L_30) gives Lsp_13 (native catches fire burning neighbour), xi2lambda(xi_inv, L_30) gives Lsp_23 (invader catches fire burning neighbour). \(\xi = 0.5\) point spread burnout equally fast: fire usually dies started, fire usually propagates. Regrowth: species' post-fire regrowth probabilities convert way, using L_01 (L_02) reference rate : eta2lambda(eta_nat, L_01) gives Lrg_01 (native long-range regrowth), eta2lambda(eta_inv, L_01) gives Lrg_02 (invader long-range regrowth). Setting L_01 = 0 therefore switches regrowth channels well ordinary native colonisation. baseline parameter set leaves native species without regrowth advantage (eta_nat = 0); eta_nat exists two species can parametrized symmetrically.

title: Convert a spread or regrowth probability to a rate constant — xi2lambda
code: # A fire-spread probability of 0.6 against a burnout rate of 1e6/year xi2lambda(0.6, 1e6) #> [1] 1500000  # xi = 0.5 returns exactly the reference rate (spread as fast as burnout) xi2lambda(0.5, 1e6) #> [1] 1e+06  # Regrowth uses L_01 as its reference rate eta2lambda(0.6, 0.03) #> [1] 0.045  # The conversion is what the simulate functions apply internally r <- default_rates() xi2lambda(r$xi_inv, r$L_30) #> [1] 1500000
